guide.title: Glastonbury, Connecticut: The Oldest Ferry in America
guide.intro: Glastonbury began in 1636 as part of Wethersfield, when 30 families settled a Connecticut River tract called Pyaug; it incorporated separately in 1693 as Glassenbury, about 7 miles southeast of Hartford across the river. The Rocky Hill-Glastonbury ferry has crossed the river since 1655 and is the oldest continually operating ferry in the United States. Glastonbury produced gunpowder during the Revolutionary War and was a shipbuilding town through the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. The J.B. Williams Company opened its Glastonbury soap factory in 1847; its Genuine Yankee Soap is credited as the first soap made expressly for shaving mugs, and the company later produced 'Lectric Shave and Aqua Velva. In the 1870s, two of the five Smith sisters, Julia and Abby — from a family active in abolition and suffrage — became national symbols of taxation without representation by refusing to pay taxes they could not vote on.

sections.heading: Pyaug to Glassenbury
sections.body: Glastonbury began in 1636 as part of Wethersfield, when 30 families settled a Connecticut River tract known by its Native name, Pyaug; it incorporated as its own town in 1693 under the name Glassenbury. The Rocky Hill-Glastonbury ferry, in service since 1655, is the oldest continually operating ferry in the United States, and Glastonbury produced gunpowder during the Revolutionary War and built ships through the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. The J.B. Williams Company opened its Glastonbury soap factory in 1847; its Genuine Yankee Soap is credited as the first soap made expressly for shaving mugs, and the company later produced 'Lectric Shave and Aqua Velva. In the 1870s, two of the five Smith sisters, Julia and Abby, refused to pay taxes on land they had no vote over, becoming national symbols of taxation without representation — part of a family also active in abolition, whose history the Museum on the Green interprets today.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Glastonbury is a drive-to town about 7 miles southeast of Hartford. The CT Route 2 expressway serves it with six exits, Route 3 links to I-91 via the Putnam Bridge over the Connecticut River, and Route 17 serves South Glastonbury. There is no rail station in Glastonbury; the nearest Amtrak and CTrail Hartford Line trains stop at Hartford Union Station. In season, the historic Rocky Hill-Glastonbury ferry carries cars across the river as well.

sections.heading: The ferry, the Museum on the Green, and Somerset Square
sections.body: The Rocky Hill-Glastonbury ferry's short crossing is still run seasonally by CTDOT — check CTroads alerts before counting on a specific day. The Museum on the Green and the 1755 Welles-Shipman-Ward House, both run by the Historical Society of Glastonbury, cover the town's colonial and Smith-sisters history. Rose's Berry Farm, picking blueberries and apples in season since 1908, sits in South Glastonbury alongside the Historical Society sites. Downtown, Daybreak Coffee Roasters has poured coffee since 1989, Bricco Trattoria serves chef Billy Grant's farm-to-table Italian, and J. Gilbert's anchors Somerset Square with wood-fired steaks. The Butternut Farm Bed & Breakfast, in a colonial house begun in 1720, is the town's verified place to stay.

faq.question: How do I get to Glastonbury?
faq.answer: Glastonbury sits about 7 miles southeast of Hartford. CT Route 2 (six exits), Route 3 via the Putnam Bridge to I-91, and Route 17 in South Glastonbury are the main roads. There's no rail station in town; the nearest Amtrak and CTrail Hartford Line service is Hartford Union Station.

faq.question: What is the Rocky Hill-Glastonbury ferry?
faq.answer: A seasonal car-and-passenger crossing of the Connecticut River run by CTDOT, operating since 1655 — the oldest continually operating ferry in the United States.

faq.question: What did the J.B. Williams Company make in Glastonbury?
faq.answer: The company opened its Glastonbury soap factory in 1847; its Genuine Yankee Soap is credited as the first soap made expressly for shaving mugs, and the company later produced 'Lectric Shave and Aqua Velva.

faq.question: Who were the Smith sisters of Glastonbury?
faq.answer: Five sisters from a family active in abolition and women's suffrage. In the 1870s, two of them, Julia and Abby, became national symbols of taxation without representation by refusing to pay taxes on land they could not vote over.

faq.question: Where can I eat and stay in Glastonbury?
faq.answer: Bricco Trattoria and J. Gilbert's Wood-Fired Steaks & Seafood anchor downtown and Somerset Square dining, with Daybreak Coffee Roasters for coffee since 1989. Butternut Farm Bed & Breakfast, in a house begun in 1720, is the town's verified lodging.

places.name: Museum on the Green
places.summary: Covers Glastonbury history from the Wangunk people through the 20th century, with permanent exhibits on Cotton Hollow and the Smith sisters. Open Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday 10 a.m.-4 p.m.

places.name: Welles-Shipman-Ward House
places.summary: A 1755 colonial house with one of the largest colonial-era hearth fireplaces in Connecticut, operated by the Historical Society of Glastonbury. Open seasonally April-October; tours arranged via 860-633-6890.

places.name: Rocky Hill-Glastonbury Ferry
places.address: Ferry landing at the foot of Ferry Lane off Main Street/Route 160, South Glastonbury
places.summary: The oldest operational ferry in the United States, in service since 1655; a short seasonal car-and-passenger crossing of the Connecticut River run by CTDOT. Check CTroads alerts before relying on a specific crossing day.

places.name: Rose's Berry Farm
places.address: 300 Matson Hill Rd, South Glastonbury, CT 06073
places.summary: A pick-your-own farm founded in 1908, offering blueberries, strawberries, raspberries, blackberries, apples, peaches, and pumpkins in season; owned by the Gondek family since 2022.

places.name: Daybreak Coffee Roasters
places.summary: Local roaster and cafe operating since 1989, serving espresso, fresh-roasted coffees, pastries, and sandwiches. Open daily 8 a.m.-4 p.m.

places.name: Bricco Trattoria
places.summary: Chef Billy Grant's farm-to-table modern Italian trattoria, operating for over a decade with daily-changing menus.

places.name: J. Gilbert's Wood-Fired Steaks & Seafood
places.summary: Wood-fired steakhouse anchoring the Somerset Square area; dinner nightly with a Sunday-Friday happy hour.

places.name: Butternut Farm Bed & Breakfast
places.summary: A B&B in a colonial house begun in 1720 by Jonathan Hale; innkeeper Don Reid opened it as a bed and breakfast in 1977 and continues as innkeeper today.
